processing: A seller describes a blend of leaf from around Menghai, with buds on the faces of the cake and medium, sturdier leaf inside; the exact recipe is not published.
harvest_season: Not sold by picking: it is a factory blend, and the batch and date on the wrapper mark production.
appearance_dry: A 357 g round cake, described by a seller as dark and glossy with neat strands and buds on the surface.
appearance_liquor: Described by a seller as deep, rich red.
appearance_wet: Typical of ripe pu-erh: soft, dark brown leaf.
taste_profile: Described by a seller as thick and deep with a clean aged aroma. Independent tasting notes are few.

brewing.notes: General ripe pu-erh approach: one quick rinse, water near the boil, short early steeps; add time gradually after the fourth steep.

vintage_note: A 2011 production, batch 101, dated 3 July 2011, is listed as a 357 g cake, seven to a stack. Release history is otherwise thin, so judge a given cake by batch, date and storage, as with other factory ripe teas.
description:
Wei Zui Yan is a Dayi ripe cake whose name promises the strongest flavour, 酽 being the Chinese word for thick, strong tea. It is a less documented cake than the factory's numbered classics.

A seller's listing describes leaf from around Menghai, with buds on the faces of the cake and sturdier leaf inside. The proportions are not published.

The reported cup is thick and deep with a clean aged aroma, which suits the name. Tasting notes are few and mostly commercial, so take them lightly. Brew as you would other ripe Menghai tea.

Check batch and date when buying, and note the alternative character 釅 on some listings, which is the same name.
history: Little is documented about when this tea first appeared or how it has changed. A batch dated July 2011 is on record, but no first release year can be confirmed.
